newsitem.title: UK: Cook puts human rights at UK foreign policy core.
newsitem.headline: Cook puts human rights at UK foreign policy core.

text.p: Human rights will be at the heart of the new British Labour government's foreign policy, Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said on Monday.

In an interview with BBC radio, Cook said Prime Minister Tony Blair's government would push for international regulation of the arms trade and support movements pressing for the sort of democratic rights that Britons takes for granted.
"I think it is very important that foreign policy is not just a matter of real politics but also has an ethical dimension," Cook said.
"We are going to put human rights at the heart of our foreign policy," he added.
Cook was speaking ahead of a news conference at which he will launch a mission statement setting out his priorities.

These include promoting national security and economic prosperity, hoisting environmental issues up the international agenda and winning respect for Britain's contribution to global peacekeeping operations.
Cook was pressed to reconcile his stress on ethics with the importance to British industry of arms sales to a number of governments with chequered human rights records.

"There are some very serious cases of flagrant human rights abuse that must be tackled. We are quite clearly establishing the principle that if we demand for Britain human rights and democratic principles and democratic government, then we must support those in other countries who are also doing the same," the foreign secretary said.
In the case of Nigeria, for example, he said Labour had a long-standing policy of supporting "tough economic sanctions on a regime which is among the most brutal in the world".
But he said the sanctions must be applied in a way that started to restore democratic rights to the people of Nigeria.
Britain, as one of the world's four leading defence exporters, would seek responsible international regulation of the arms trade through an eight-point plan, Cook said.
"In particular, we are going to press for a European Union code of conduct to make sure that if we say No, this export is wrong'... no other European company then takes up that contract," he said.
Cook launched a high-profile charm offensive last week with trips to Paris and Bonn to underscore Britain's determination to make a new start in its dealings with the European Union.
But he denied that the emphasis on mending fences with Europe meant that transatlantic ties would be neglected.
"It is a false dichotomy that you have to choose Europe or America. The truth of the matter is that Washington does not want a Britain that is marginalised offshore from Europe," Cook said.
